To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) The glutamate receptor ligands binding domain (S1S2) undergoes a load and lock cleft‐closing conformational transition; 2) The S1S2 cleft opening transition is driven by the disruption of the hydrogen bonds between the two lobed of the protein, while the cleft‐closure is stabilized by a salt bridge between E705 and K730; 3) The S652 peptide bond is not essential to the conformational transition,

(1) the S652 peptide flip in the GluR2 ligand binding domain is not the main driving force for the cleft opening transition, (2) the electrostatic interactions between residues E705 and K730 are important in stabilizing the closed state of GluR, and (3) the cleft opening/closing transition in GluR2 S1 S2 is not a mechanical hinge mechanism, but rather it can be described as load and lock.
The cleft closure con-formational transition in GluR2 S1 S2 is not a hinge-type mechanism.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structural and dynamical properties of the ligand binding domains (LBD) of the ionotropic glutamate receptors (iGluR).
the molecular mechanism of conformational transition of GluR S1S2.
the structural rigidity of the ligand bindingdomain of the GluR2 ion channel, and the role of electrostatic interactions in stabilizing the closed conformation of the cleft between two protein lobes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the cleft closure is a load and lock transition, where the cleft is opened when two cross‐binding site hydrogen bonds are disrupted, and then the protein is locked in the open conformation due to the loss of a salt bridge between E705 and K730.
the S1S2 protein undergoes a conformational transition that involves both electrostatic and steric interactions, with the former being more significant.
the S1S2 domain of the GluR2 receptor undergoes a conformational transition from an open to a closed state upon ligand binding.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cleft‐opening transition in GluR2 S1 S2 can be characterized as load and lock mechanism and is not hinge type.
we have identified the key residues in the S1S2 domain that are responsible for its cleft‐closure mechanism.

the structural flexibility of GluR ligand binding domain is not a prerequisite for its conformational transitions, and the cleft closure transition is driven by electrostatic interactions rather than mechanical hinges.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the cleft‐opening mechanism of GluR ligand binding domain is a hinge‐like, load‐and‐lock mechanism, where the load is provided by the electrostatic interactions of the E705 residue with the K730 residue, and the lock is provided by the cross‐cleft H‐bonds between S1 and S2 subdomains.
the cleft‐opening transition in S1S2 can be described as a load and release mechanism, where the load is the electrostatic interaction between the E705‐R730 and E706‐K730 pairs of residues.

in order to understand the role of the protein flexibility in ligand binding it is necessary to consider not only the flexibility/flexibility of the protein, but also the interplay of the flexibility/flexiblity and electrostatic interactions.
